newsitem.title: USA: GM facing Friday strike deadline in Ft. Wayne, Ind..
newsitem.headline: GM facing Friday strike deadline in Ft. Wayne, Ind..

text.p: Three months after General Motors Corp. finished a rocky season of national labor talks, the automaker is facing its first local strike deadline, marking what could be a turbulent spring for labor relations.

Members of United Auto Workers Local 2209 were given permission last week by union leaders in Detroit to strike GM's pickup truck assembly plant in Ft. Wayne, Ind., at 10 a.m. Friday if a new contract is not reached.

About 2,700 UAW members work at the plant, which makes about 1,000 GM's Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra regular cab full-size pickup trucks a day. The plant runs two eight-hour shifts a day, in addition to overtime, said GM spokesman Tom Beaman.

Union officials have said they want the company to hire more workers and address health and safety issues. A spokesman for Local 2209 said Monday talks were continuing. He declined to comment further because of a news blackout.

Unlike some light truck products that are in short supply, a strike at the plant would not immediately hurt dealers. The C/K and Sierra pickup trucks overall had a more than 90 days supply at the beginning of February -- higher than the 60 days supply the industry considers to be ideal.

UAW members ratified a new three-year national agreement with GM last fall, following a series of strikes that cost the company about $700 million in lost profits. GM still has to hammer out separate pacts with its 105 local bargaining units.
So far, about 60 percent of those locals have reached agreements. Talks at the remaining 40 percent are continuing at a slow pace, analysts and union officials say.

Local leaders at several other GM assembly plants have either asked UAW leaders to authorize strikes, or are involved in tense negotiations that could lead to that. Those facilities include car plants in Oklahoma City, Okla., and Lordstown, Ohio; and the pickup truck plant in Pontiac, Mich.

UAW spokesman Reg McGhee said the union does not comment on its local negotiations. GM spokesman Charles Licari said it would be inaccurate to say talks have bogged down. Because the national agreement bargaining stretched into November, he said many of the local negotiations did not intensify until after the first of the year.
"The main thing is everybody is talking and continuing their discussions," he said.

David Cole, director of the University of Michigan's Center for the Study of Automotive Transportation, believes GM would be willing to take a strike in Ft. Wayne and at other assembly plants in order to hang on to the gains it achieved in the new national labor agreement.

The pact allows GM to permanently cut jobs it is able to eliminate through productivity gains. GM has about 210,000 UAW workers now, and hopes to reduce that by about 30,000 through attrition by the end of the current contract. If it achieves that level, Cole estimates the company could save $2 billion by the end of the contract in 1999.
At places like Ft. Wayne, which will get the next generation of pickup truck next year, GM is looking to slash its labor costs by about 30 percent, Cole said.
"The last thing the company wants to do is add people to reduce overtime, and when the new truck comes in, sit there with all these people they don't know what to do with," he said.
Meanwhile, the UAW's McGhee disputed a National Labor Relations Board complaint filed against Local 1853 at GM's Saturn Corp. plant in Spring Hill, Tenn.

The NLRB regional director filed the complaint last week, alleging the union has established a re-initiation fee for people who leave the union and then want to rejoin the bargaining unit. Labor friction at the Saturn plant is unusual because the facility is often mentioned by industry analysts as a model of cooperation between the automaker and the union.
